Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a common fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis. It affects leaves, blossoms, and developing fruit, leading to premature leaf fall and blemished, cracked apples.
symptoms: Velvety, olive-green to dark brown circular spots on leaves
Affected leaf spots become scabby, thickened, and puckered over time
Premature yellowing and dropping of infected leaves
Brown, corky, cracked scabs on the surface of maturing apples
possible_causes: Fungus Venturia inaequalis surviving through winter in fallen leaves
Cool, wet spring weather with prolonged periods of leaf moisture (dew or rain)
Dense tree canopies with restricted airflow and limited sunlight penetration
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars suitable for your region
Prune trees annually during dormancy to open the canopy for better air circulation and sunlight
Rake, chop, or safely compost/destroy fallen leaves in autumn to minimize overwintering spores
Water the root zone rather than using overhead sprinklers that wet foliage
care_recommendations: Inspect trees weekly during early spring from bud break through early fruit set
Ensure proper tree spacing and weed control beneath the canopy to reduce ground humidity
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that promotes overly dense, vulnerable leafy growth
safe_treatment: Organic options include preventive sulfur sprays or copper-based bio-fungicides applied at green tip stage before blossoming
If severe and synthetic fungicides are needed, consult your local agricultural extension service for registered products and adhere strictly to label instructions and harvest waiting periods
Do not apply copper sprays during bloom or in cold, wet conditions to avoid fruit russeting

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It attacks leaves (causing frogeye leaf spots), branches (producing sunken cankers), and fruit (causing dark, firm concentric rot).
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves expanding into circular 'frogeye' lesions with tan centers and purple borders
Firm, brown rotting zones on fruit expanding in concentric dark rings
Infected fruit shrivels and turns into a hard black 'mummy' that may hang on the tree
Sunken, reddish-brown cankers on twigs and main limbs
possible_causes: Fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa overwintering in dead wood, pruning stubs, and mummified fruit
Warm, humid conditions (20–27°C) accompanied by frequent rains
Bark wounds caused by pruning, hail, sunscald, or fire blight cankers
prevention: Prune out dead, broken, cankered, or diseased branches during dry dormant weather
Collect and dispose of all mummified apples from trees and the orchard floor before spring
Disinfect pruning tools with 70% alcohol or 10% bleach solution between cuts
Prevent bark injuries and manage insect pests that wound fruit
care_recommendations: Maintain general tree health through balanced nutrition and proper irrigation
Prune to promote fast drying of foliage and fruit after rains
Scout orchards promptly after bloom for early signs of leaf spotting
safe_treatment: Apply protective captan or copper-based sprays starting from early bloom through petal fall if disease pressure was high previously
Pruning dead wood is often more effective than chemical sprays alone
Follow all regional safety regulations, label application rates, and pre-harvest intervals

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is a fungal disease caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It requires two alternate host plants—apples and eastern red cedar/juniper—to complete its two-year life cycle.
symptoms: Small, pale yellow spots on the upper leaf surface that enlarge and turn bright orange-yellow
Tiny black specks form in the center of orange leaf spots
Small, cup- or tube-like fungal structures appear on the underside of infected leaves in summer
Premature leaf drop and occasional distorted spots on developing fruit
possible_causes: Spores blown by wind from swollen brown galls on nearby juniper or red cedar trees during spring rains
Prolonged leaf wetness during warm spring rains (15–24°C)
Presence of susceptible juniper hosts within 500 meters to 1 kilometer of apple orchards
prevention: Plant rust-resistant or rust-immune apple varieties where rust is prevalent
Where practical, remove wild cedar or juniper trees within 500 meters of the apple orchard
Prune and destroy brown galls on nearby ornamental junipers before warm spring rains release spores
care_recommendations: Monitor apple foliage closely during the 4 to 6 weeks following bud break
Keep trees pruned for adequate airflow to minimize moisture duration on leaves
Collect and compost or bury fallen rust-affected foliage
safe_treatment: Apply labeled protective fungicides or wettable sulfur starting at pink bud stage through petal fall during rainy periods
Chemical treatments are only effective as protectants before infection occurs; they cannot cure spots once visible
Always consult your local agricultural extension service for recommended spray timings and safety guidelines

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage displays uniform green color, intact leaf margins, and clear venation with no signs of fungal spotting, rust pustules, or bacterial lesions.
symptoms: No visible lesions, spots, or powdery mildew coatings
Vigorous, balanced leaf growth with healthy green coloration
Intact leaf surface and unblemished petioles
possible_causes: Good orchard hygiene, balanced tree nutrition, and favorable weather conditions
prevention: Continue annual dormant pruning to maintain canopy ventilation
Maintain clean orchard floor and manage weeds around tree bases
Inspect regularly for seasonal pests like aphids, mites, and leafhoppers
care_recommendations: Provide consistent moisture to the root zone during fruit bulking
Apply organic mulch around the dripline to conserve soil moisture and moderate root temperature
Conduct routine soil or foliar nutrient tests every 2 to 3 years
safe_treatment: No chemical treatment is needed. Continue routine preventive cultural care

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry leaves exhibit healthy, deep green foliage, smooth edges, and vigorous new shoot growth with no chlorosis, scorch, or spots.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf color with no interveinal yellowing (iron chlorosis)
No fungal spots, powdery mold, or twig blight symptoms
Firm, supple leaf blades and strong terminal shoot growth
possible_causes: Optimal acidic soil pH (4.5–5.5), steady hydration, and proper organic mulching
prevention: Maintain soil acidity within the ideal pH range using elemental sulfur or organic pine mulch if needed
Ensure excellent soil drainage; blueberries are sensitive to waterlogged roots
Prune out weak, spindly, or older unproductive canes in late winter
care_recommendations: Water regularly with clean, low-sodium water using drip irrigation
Replenish a 5–10 cm layer of pine bark, wood chips, or pine needle mulch annually
Use fertilizers formulated specifically for acid-loving plants (ammonium sulfate or urea)
safe_treatment: No treatment necessary. Maintain acidic soil and root moisture

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Cherry powdery mildew is caused by Podosphaera clandestina. It affects leaves and green fruit stems, covering tender tissues with a white talcum-like fungal coating and distorting foliage.
symptoms: White, powdery or felt-like fungal patches appearing on young leaves and terminal shoots
Leaves curl upward, cup, or become leathery, distorted, and stunted
Infected leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely
Powdery white growth can develop on ripening cherry fruit surfaces
possible_causes: Fungus Podosphaera clandestina overwintering in bud scales and fallen leaf litter
Warm days (15–28°C) combined with humid nights and shady canopy interiors
Over-fertilization with nitrogen causing excessive tender vegetative growth
prevention: Prune the tree canopy annually to allow bright sunlight and breeze into the center
Avoid overhead irrigation that creates high humidity inside dense foliage
Balance nitrogen fertilizer to avoid surges of tender, vulnerable late-season shoots
care_recommendations: Prune off and safely discard heavily infected shoot tips early in the spring
Maintain weed-free ground under the tree to encourage dry airflow
Water deeply at the base during dry periods to prevent moisture stress
safe_treatment: Apply horticultural mineral oils, potassium bicarbonate, or neem oil at the first sign of mildew
Sulfur sprays provide effective preventive protection, but do not apply sulfur when temperatures exceed 30°C to avoid leaf burn
Consult local extension guidelines for approved fungicides in commercial orchards

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: The cherry foliage shows rich green coloration, crisp serrated margins, and clean leaf surfaces free of mildew, shot-hole perforations, or leaf curling.
symptoms: Vibrant, dark green foliage with intact, saw-toothed margins
No white powdery coatings, yellowing, or bacterial shot-holes
Strong petiole attachments and vigorous shoot extension
possible_causes: Favorable weather, balanced pruning, proper watering, and effective pest management
prevention: Prune during dry summer weather to reduce the risk of bacterial canker infection
Maintain a consistent irrigation schedule during fruit development
Monitor regularly for cherry fruit fly, aphids, and early leaf diseases
care_recommendations: Apply organic mulch around the dripline while keeping mulch away from the trunk
Fertilize lightly after harvest if tree growth needs support based on soil tests
Protect developing fruit from birds using protective orchard netting
safe_treatment: No chemical intervention required. Continue good orchard management

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is a foliar fungal disease caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It creates distinctive rectangular lesions bounded by leaf veins, reducing photosynthetic area and grain yield.
symptoms: Small, tan, halo-like spots that expand into long, narrow rectangular lesions (1–6 cm)
Lesions are sharply bounded by parallel leaf veins, giving them a rectangular or blocky shape
Lesions turn grayish-tan as spores develop in humid conditions
Blended lesions cause extensive blighting, stalk lodging, and premature plant death
possible_causes: Fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis surviving in corn residue on the soil surface
Warm temperatures (24–30°C) combined with high humidity and prolonged dew periods
Continuous corn-on-corn planting and minimal tillage systems that leave abundant surface crop debris
prevention: Rotate crops for at least 1–2 years with non-host crops like soybeans, sorghum, or legumes
Select resistant or moderately resistant corn hybrid varieties
Tillage to bury corn debris where soil conservation practices permit
care_recommendations: Avoid overly high planting densities that restrict air circulation in the field
Maintain adequate soil potassium and balanced nitrogen fertility
Scout lower leaves beginning two weeks prior to silking
safe_treatment: Apply foliar fungicides only when economic thresholds are met (e.g. lesions on third leaf below the ear leaf at silking)
Consult local agricultural extension guidelines for regional fungicide efficacy and timing
Always follow product label restrictions regarding growth stage limits and grazing intervals

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It is characterized by powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces, spread by wind-borne spores over long distances.
symptoms: Small, powdery, circular to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules scattered across both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing powdery reddish-brown spores
Pustules turn brownish-black late in the season as resting spores form
Severe infections lead to leaf chlorosis, partial defoliation, and decreased grain fill
possible_causes: Airborne spores blown northward or into fields by prevailing storm systems
Moderate temperatures (16–25°C) coupled with high relative humidity and nighttime dew
Susceptible sweet corn varieties or inbred seed corn lines
prevention: Plant corn hybrid varieties with known resistance to Puccinia sorghi
Plant early in the season to escape peak late-summer spore migrations
Provide balanced soil nutrition to support natural plant resilience
care_recommendations: Scout fields periodically, especially during prolonged cool, cloudy weather spells
Field corn usually tolerates moderate rust without significant economic yield loss
Manage field weeds to maximize air circulation across the crop canopy
safe_treatment: Fungicide treatment is rarely justified for commercial field corn unless severe infection occurs before tasseling
For high-value sweet corn or seed production, labeled fungicides may be applied if pustules threaten upper leaves early
Check local university extension thresholds and adhere strictly to label safety guidelines

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern corn leaf blight is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. It forms large, cigar-shaped grayish-green lesions that can severely reduce photosynthetic leaf area during grain filling.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green or tan lesions (2.5–15 cm long) on leaves
Lesions expand across leaf veins and develop dark, velvety fungal spore clusters in damp weather
In severe outbreaks, lesions coalesce to give the canopy a frosted or burnt appearance
Premature death of entire leaves, leading to reduced grain yield and weakened stalks
possible_causes: Fungus Exserohilum turcicum overwintering on infested corn residue
Moderate temperatures (18–27°C) accompanied by extended periods of leaf wetness (6–18 hours)
Monoculture corn cropping with minimal residue management
prevention: Plant corn hybrids containing specific resistance genes (e.g. Ht genes) or high multi-genic tolerance
Rotate fields with non-grass crops such as soybeans, pulses, or brassicas for 1 to 2 seasons
Manage surface corn residue through light tillage or chopping where erosion management allows
care_recommendations: Scout lower leaves every 7–10 days from early whorl stage through early reproductive stages
Maintain balanced fertility; avoid potassium deficiency which increases blight vulnerability
Ensure proper field drainage to reduce microclimate humidity
safe_treatment: Consider registered foliar fungicides if lesions appear on the ear leaf or above during silking on susceptible hybrids
Applications after dent stage provide little economic benefit
Consult agricultural extension advisors for current local fungicide efficacy ratings and follow label safety intervals

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The corn leaf displays vigorous, deep green coloration, distinct parallel veins, and strong leaf margins with no signs of fungal blights, rust pustules, or insect feeding.
symptoms: Uniform, healthy green color with clear linear venation
No elongated cigar-shaped lesions, rectangular spots, or powdery pustules
Supple, broad leaf blade without leaf tearing or insect chewing
possible_causes: Resistant hybrid seed, good crop rotation, balanced soil nutrients, and appropriate moisture
prevention: Continue crop rotation practices with soybeans or other non-grasses
Maintain timely field scouting throughout vegetative and reproductive stages
Control early season weeds that compete for water and nutrients
care_recommendations: Ensure adequate water availability during critical tasseling and silking windows
Apply nitrogen side-dressing at recommended growth stages based on soil test targets
Monitor soil moisture and scout for stem borers or armyworms
safe_treatment: No chemical intervention needed. Maintain sound agronomic management

Grape___Black_rot.description: Grape black rot is caused by Guignardia bidwellii. It is a major fungal threat in warm, humid grape-growing regions, causing leaf spots, shoot lesions, and shriveled black mummified berries.
symptoms: Small, circular reddish-brown leaf spots with distinct dark brown margins
Tiny black pimple-like fruiting bodies (pycnidia) arranged in rings inside the leaf spots
Infected berries turn pale, soften, decay, and shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies
Black, elongated cankers on young canes, tendrils, and leaf stalks
possible_causes: Fungus Guignardia bidwellii overwintering in mummified berries on vines or the vineyard floor
Warm temperatures (21–32°C) combined with frequent rain and high relative humidity
Dense canopy shading that prevents morning dew from evaporating rapidly
prevention: Remove and destroy all mummified grape clusters during winter pruning
Prune and train vines to open canopies for maximum sunlight and airflow
Keep vineyard floor vegetation and weeds closely mown to reduce humidity
Plant black rot-resistant grape cultivars where feasible
care_recommendations: Perform early-season shoot positioning and leaf pulling around grape clusters after bloom
Avoid sprinkler irrigation that wets grape foliage; use drip lines along vine rows
Scout young leaves and berry clusters weekly beginning at early shoot growth
safe_treatment: Apply protective copper, sulfur, or registered protective fungicides starting when new shoots are 5–15 cm long through 4–6 weeks post-bloom
Berry clusters are most susceptible from bloom until pea-sized; protection during this window is vital
Adhere strictly to pre-harvest intervals and label safety requirements

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca (black measles) is a complex fungal trunk disease caused by a combination of fungi (including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium minimum). It degrades the vine vascular system and wood.
symptoms: Characteristic 'tiger-stripe' leaf pattern with yellow or red chlorotic bands between green veins
Leaf tissue inside the colored bands becomes brown and necrotic (scorched appearance)
Berries develop small, dark brown to purple speckles or measles across the skin
Sudden midsummer wilting and collapse of shoots or whole vines (apoplexy) during hot weather
possible_causes: Fungi invading woody tissues through pruning wounds and mechanical injuries
Aging vineyards (typically appearing in vines older than 8–10 years)
Heat and water stress accelerating the collapse of compromised vascular vessels
prevention: Make clean pruning cuts and avoid large trunk wounds whenever possible
Prune late in the dormant season during dry, sunny weather when wound healing is faster
Apply wound protectant paints, pastes, or biocontrol agents (Trichoderma) to fresh pruning cuts
Disinfect pruning shears regularly between vines with disinfectant solutions
care_recommendations: Mark symptomatic vines in summer for separate pruning or trunk renewal during winter
Manage vineyard irrigation carefully to prevent extreme water stress during hot spells
Consider trunk renewal by training a healthy sucker from the base of affected vines
safe_treatment: There are no curative chemical sprays once fungal wood rot is established within the trunk
Management relies entirely on preventive sanitation, wound protection, and trunk surgical renewal
Consult a viticultural extension specialist before undertaking major vine removal

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Grape leaf blight, caused by Pseudocercospora cladosporioides (Isariopsis cladosporioides), is a late-season foliar disease that causes irregular leaf necrosis and early defoliation.
symptoms: Small, irregular, circular to angular dark reddish-brown to black spots on leaves
Spots may develop faint yellowish halos around margins on older leaves
Fungal spots coalesce, causing large dead patches and premature leaf drop
Defoliation weakens vines, reducing winter hardiness and next season's bud fruitfulness
possible_causes: Fungus overwintering in fallen leaves and dormant vine bark crevices
Warm, humid conditions and late-season rainfall or prolonged dew
Dense, shaded canopy interiors with restricted airflow
prevention: Prune and train vines to maintain an open canopy with good air movement
Rake or incorporate fallen leaves after autumn harvest to reduce spore reservoirs
Manage shoot density through selective shoot thinning in spring
care_recommendations: Irrigate through drip systems to avoid wetting leaves
Ensure balanced fertilization; avoid late nitrogen applications that delay vine dormancy
Scout older, lower leaves inside the canopy during late summer
safe_treatment: Routine vineyard post-bloom copper or sulfur sprays generally provide good suppression
If severe late-season blight occurs, consult local viticultural authorities for approved foliar treatments
Observe label safety directions and pre-harvest intervals if treating prior to grape harvest

Grape___healthy.description: The grapevine leaf shows lush, vibrant green tissue, characteristic leaf lobing, and clear veins without spots, downy mildew patches, or leaf scorch.
symptoms: Uniform, healthy green color across leaf lobes
No tiger-stripe chlorosis, black rot spots, or powdery mildew coatings
Clean leaf petioles and healthy, vigorous tendril growth
possible_causes: Proper canopy trellising, balanced vine nutrition, good drainage, and proactive orchard sanitation
prevention: Continue regular shoot positioning, tucking, and selective summer leaf pulling
Maintain weed-free vine strips to encourage airflow and discourage pests
Monitor weekly for leafhoppers, thrips, and powdery mildew signs
care_recommendations: Irrigate according to vine water requirements, reducing water slightly during veraison
Conduct petiole nutrient analysis at bloom or veraison to calibrate fertilizer programs
Keep grapevine cordon and trunk free of mechanical tractor wounds
safe_treatment: No chemical treatment necessary. Maintain good viticultural practices

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB) or Citrus Greening is a devastating bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid. It causes asymmetric leaf mottling, bitter lopsided fruit, and gradual tree decline.
symptoms: Asymmetrical, blotchy, mottled yellowing across leaf blades (yellowing does not mirror on both sides of the midrib)
Thickened, raised, corky leaf veins with an upright 'rabbit ears' leaf posture
Small, lopsided, bitter-tasting fruit that fails to color properly (remains green at the bottom)
Heavy premature fruit drop, twig dieback, and general canopy thinning
possible_causes: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus spread by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri)
Propagation using infected budwood or graft material
Movement of infected nursery plants between geographical regions
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free citrus trees from registered, insect-screened nurseries
Regularly monitor and aggressively control Asian citrus psyllid populations using sticky traps and scouting
Quarantine and never transport citrus plant material from known HLB-endemic areas
Promptly remove and safely destroy confirmed HLB-infected trees to protect neighboring citrus groves
care_recommendations: Provide enhanced foliar nutrition (zinc, iron, manganese, boron) and consistent irrigation to support declining trees
Coordinate psyllid control measures cooperatively with neighboring orchard owners
Immediately report suspected symptoms to local agricultural extension and plant health officers
safe_treatment: There is no known cure for Candidatus Liberibacter once a tree is infected
Chemical treatments are strictly directed at controlling the insect vector (psyllids) using registered insecticides
Follow all local regulatory directives for quarantined citrus diseases

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It causes water-soaked angular leaf spots, shot-hole perforations, premature defoliation, and cracked fruit blemishes.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown or black
The diseased centers of leaf spots drop out, producing a characteristic 'shot-hole' appearance
Severely infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, starting at the shoot tips
Small, sunken, dark brown spots on peaches that crack and exude gum
possible_causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni overwintering in twig cankers and bud scales
Warm, humid, windy conditions with blowing sand or rain that wounds tender leaf tissue
Planting in sandy, wind-exposed soils without adequate windbreaks
prevention: Plant bacterial spot-resistant peach cultivars adapted to your growing area
Establish windbreaks or cover crops in sandy orchards to reduce wind-blown particle abrasions
Avoid excessive summer pruning or late nitrogen applications that stimulate late tender growth
care_recommendations: Avoid overhead irrigation; water via drip lines under the tree canopy
Prune out infected twigs and cankers during dormant winter pruning
Maintain moderate, steady tree growth with balanced fertilization
safe_treatment: Apply dormant or early-season copper sprays before bud break to reduce bacterial inoculum
Low-rate copper or registered bactericides (oxytetracycline) may be applied in-season under agricultural extension guidance
Exercise extreme caution with in-season copper sprays on peaches because peach foliage is highly sensitive to copper phytotoxicity

Peach___healthy.description: The peach leaf displays healthy, elongated lance-like foliage with bright green color, crisp margins, and no shot-holes, leaf curl, or cankers.
symptoms: Smooth, lanceolate green leaf blades without spots or perforations
No curling, puckering, or reddish blistered distortions (peach leaf curl)
Clean shoots and healthy terminal buds
possible_causes: Good orchard hygiene, dormant disease sprays, appropriate pruning, and adequate irrigation
prevention: Apply standard dormant copper or lime-sulfur sprays before bud swell to prevent peach leaf curl
Prune annually in late winter to maintain an open-center vase tree shape
Monitor regularly for oriental fruit moth, peach tree borer, and aphids
care_recommendations: Thin fruit early in the season to maintain fruit size and tree vigor
Mulch around the base with organic material, keeping mulch away from the root collar
Provide deep watering during dry spells, especially during fruit sizing
safe_treatment: No chemical treatment needed. Continue routine seasonal orchard maintenance

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on bell peppers is caused by Xanthomonas species. It is a damaging disease that causes small water-soaked leaf spots, extensive defoliation, and raised wart-like scabs on pepper fruit.
symptoms: Small, circular to angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown to black
Spots may develop yellow chlorotic margins
Severe infection leads to widespread leaf yellowing and heavy leaf drop, exposing fruit to sunscald
Raised, circular, rough, scab-like spots on green and red bell peppers
possible_causes: Infected seed or infected commercial transplants
Bacterium Xanthomonas surviving in crop residues and weeds in the nightshade family
Warm temperatures (24–30°C) with splashing rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and disease-resistant bell pepper hybrids (with race-specific resistance)
Rotate crops for at least 2–3 years with non-solanaceous crops (e.g. sweetcorn, beans, brassicas)
Sanitize seedling flats, greenhouse benches, and garden stakes with disinfectant solutions
Never work among or harvest wet pepper plants to prevent spreading bacteria
care_recommendations: Use drip irrigation under plastic or organic mulch rather than overhead sprinkler watering
Ensure wide plant spacing to improve sunlight and facilitate quick leaf drying
Promptly rogue out and destroy heavily infected seedlings before transplanting
safe_treatment: Apply preventive copper bactericide sprays combined with mancozeb early in the season before disease becomes widespread
Bio-pesticides containing Bacillus subtilis or bacteriophages may provide protective suppression
Chemical sprays have limited effectiveness once disease is widespread; focus primarily on sanitation and resistance

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: The bell pepper foliage exhibits smooth, rich green, glossy leaves with clean edges and strong stems, free from water-soaked spots, mosaic mottling, or wilt.
symptoms: Smooth, vibrant green leaf surface without spots, scabs, or yellowing
No curling, mosaic mottling, or insect webbing
Firm, upright plant stems and healthy flower bud development
possible_causes: Healthy disease-free transplants, balanced soil nutrition, proper drip irrigation, and weed control
prevention: Maintain crop rotation away from peppers, tomatoes, and eggplants
Mulch soil around plants to preserve moisture and suppress weeds
Scout weekly for aphids, thrips, and pepper hornworms
care_recommendations: Ensure regular watering to prevent blossom end rot caused by calcium-moisture imbalances
Stake or cage pepper plants to support heavy fruit loads and keep branches off the soil
Apply balanced fertilizer with adequate phosphorus and potassium for fruit development
safe_treatment: No treatment required. Maintain standard crop care

Potato___Early_blight.description: Potato early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It targets older foliage first, producing dark circular lesions with target-like concentric rings that gradually kill lower leaves.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots starting on older lower leaves
Lesions develop characteristic concentric rings resembling a target or bullseye pattern
Yellowing (chlorosis) develops around the lesions, eventually causing whole leaflets to wither and drop
Dark, sunken, dry, leathery lesions on the surface of harvested potato tubers
possible_causes: Fungus Alternaria solani surviving in crop debris, volunteer potatoes, or solanaceous weeds
Alternating wet and dry weather conditions with warm temperatures (24–29°C)
Plant stress caused by heavy tuber load, poor nitrogen fertility, or drought
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes
Rotate crops for at least 3 years away from potatoes, tomatoes, and eggplants
Maintain optimal plant nutrition, particularly nitrogen and potassium, to prevent premature vine senescence
care_recommendations: Water with drip irrigation or water early in the morning so foliage dries quickly
Hill potatoes well to provide loose soil cover over developing tubers and protect them from spores washed by rain
Remove volunteer potato sprouts emerging in neighboring rotation fields
safe_treatment: Apply protective copper fungicides or registered bio-fungicides when lower leaves first show symptoms
In commercial fields, consult local extension spray schedules using registered protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil or mancozeb)
Observe label safety directions, pre-harvest intervals, and resistance management rotations

Potato___Late_blight.description: Potato late blight is an aggressive disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It spreads with extreme speed in cool, damp weather, causing large dark water-soaked lesions and devastating crop loss.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked dark green to purplish-black lesions on leaves and stems
Delicate white, fuzzy mold growth visible on the underside of leaves around lesion borders in humid conditions
Rapid collapse, browning, and rotting of entire foliage canopies, often accompanied by an odor
Tubers develop a patchy brown-to-purple dry rot on the skin and granular brown decay in flesh
possible_causes: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans overwintering in infected seed tubers, cull piles, or volunteer potatoes
Cool (10–21°C), foggy, overcast weather with high humidity (>90%) and frequent rain or heavy dew
Airborne spores transported by wind over distances of several kilometers during cloudy periods
prevention: Plant only certified late blight-free seed potatoes and choose blight-tolerant cultivars where available
Eliminate all potato cull piles and volunteer potatoes before the growing season starts
Avoid planting potatoes immediately adjacent to tomato crops
Avoid overhead irrigation; schedule irrigation to allow complete canopy drying before nightfall
care_recommendations: Hill potato rows thoroughly to create a deep soil buffer that blocks spores from reaching tubers
Scout fields at least twice weekly during cool, damp weather periods
Kill and allow vines to desiccate completely at least two weeks before harvesting tubers
safe_treatment: Immediate preventive treatment is essential before disease takes hold; curative options are very limited
Apply protective copper fungicides or registered late-blight fungicides based on local disease warning systems
If late blight is confirmed on isolated plants, carefully bag, pull, and destroy them immediately to prevent field-wide destruction
Report outbreaks to regional agricultural extension authorities

Potato___healthy.description: The potato leaf displays healthy, deep green compound foliage, robust stems, and clean leaflet margins free of blight lesions, target spots, or insect chewing.
symptoms: Vigorous, dark green compound leaves with intact leaflet edges
No water-soaked spots, concentric target rings, or white underside mold
Sturdy green stems supporting balanced vegetative growth
possible_causes: Certified clean seed, proper hill cultivation, consistent moisture, and good crop rotation
prevention: Continue hilling soil around the base of the plants as they grow
Maintain crop rotation away from solanaceous plants for at least 3 years
Monitor weekly for Colorado potato beetles, potato aphids, and early blight signs
care_recommendations: Maintain steady soil moisture especially during flowering and tuber bulking
Avoid waterlogging which can trigger root rots and tuber suffocation
Ensure balanced fertilization with adequate potassium and phosphorus
safe_treatment: No chemical treatment necessary. Maintain standard good cultural practices

Raspberry___healthy.description: The raspberry leaf exhibits healthy, compound serrated foliage with vibrant green upper surfaces, characteristic whitish-green undersides, and no fungal spots or cane lesions.
symptoms: Compound leaves with crisp, green, serrated leaflet edges
Clean leaf undersides free of orange rust pustules or powdery mildew
Vigorous new cane growth (primocanes) with strong petioles
possible_causes: Well-drained soil, organic mulching, proper cane trellising, and good annual pruning
prevention: Prune out floricanes (fruiting canes) immediately after harvest to improve airflow for primocanes
Maintain a 5–10 cm organic mulch layer to keep roots cool and preserve moisture
Provide trellis support to keep canes off the ground and oriented toward sunlight
care_recommendations: Water deeply with drip irrigation around the root zone
Ensure excellent soil drainage; raspberries are highly prone to Phytophthora root rot in soggy soils
Monitor periodically for spider mites and cane borers
safe_treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine cane management

Soybean___healthy.description: The soybean leaf exhibits healthy trifoliolate foliage with uniform green coloration, strong veins, and fine surface hairs, free of rust pustules, bacterial pustules, or mosaic mottling.
symptoms: Even, healthy green trifoliolate leaves with unblemished leaflet margins
No chlorotic mottling, angular water-soaked spots, or rust pustules
Firm petiole attachments and vigorous nodulating vegetative growth
possible_causes: Certified clean seed, proper Bradyrhizobium seed inoculation, good soil drainage, and timely weed management
prevention: Rotate crops annually with corn, sorghum, or small grains
Plant resistant seed varieties adapted to your maturity zone
Scout fields periodically for early defoliators and soybean rust spores
care_recommendations: Ensure good soil fertility, particularly phosphorus and potassium
Maintain weed-free canopy closure to reduce weed competition and conserve moisture
Check roots early in the season to confirm active pink nitrogen-fixing root nodules
safe_treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine agronomic management

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on squash is caused by Podosphaera xanthii (or Golovinomyces cichoracearum). It forms talc-like white fungal patches on leaves and stems, causing premature defoliation and poor fruit development.
symptoms: White, talcum-like powdery spots appearing first on older lower leaves and shaded leaf undersides
Spots rapidly expand into large powdery patches covering entire leaf blades and petioles
Infected leaves turn yellow, brown, become crisp, and die prematurely
Loss of protective foliage leads to fruit sunscald, reduced sugars, and incomplete fruit ripening
possible_causes: Fungal spores transported by wind from neighboring cucurbit fields or weeds
Warm temperatures (20–28°C) combined with high relative humidity in shaded canopies
Dense planting, low light intensity, and lack of air movement around foliage
prevention: Select powdery mildew-resistant squash varieties (labeled PMR)
Space plants widely to maximize air circulation and sunlight penetration
Plant in full sun locations with well-drained soil
Clean up and safely dispose of infected crop residues at the end of the season
care_recommendations: Water at the soil level using drip irrigation; keep leaves as dry as possible
Prune out surrounding weeds that shade the squash bed and raise microclimate humidity
Scout older, shaded leaves weekly beginning at mid-season
safe_treatment: Apply potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or horticultural oils at the earliest sign of white fungal spots
Bio-fungicides based on Bacillus subtilis or sulfur can provide preventive protection (avoid sulfur on sulfur-sensitive cucurbit varieties or when temperatures exceed 30°C)
For severe commercial infestations, consult agricultural extension recommendations for approved systemic fungicides with alternating modes of action

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Strawberry leaf scorch is caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. It produces numerous purplish spots on upper leaf surfaces that coalesce, causing leaf margins to curl and look scorched by fire.
symptoms: Numerous small, irregular, purple to dark reddish-purple spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots lack the pale white centers typical of common leaf spot; they remain dark throughout
Spots enlarge and merge, causing leaves to turn brown, curl upward at the edges, and appear burned or scorched
Severe infection can weaken crown vigor and reduce next season's runner production and yield
possible_causes: Fungus Diplocarpon earlianum overwintering on infected older strawberry leaves
Frequent rainfall or overhead sprinkler watering that keeps leaves wet for prolonged hours
Warm to moderate temperatures (15–25°C) and overcrowded strawberry beds
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant strawberry cultivars
Plant on raised beds with proper plant spacing to facilitate rapid drying of leaves
Renovate strawberry beds after harvest by mowing old foliage and removing old debris
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation placed under straw or plastic mulch
care_recommendations: Remove and discard heavily scorched older leaves during post-harvest cleanup
Keep strawberry beds free of weeds that restrict air circulation
Apply balanced fertilizer after renovation rather than heavy spring applications
safe_treatment: Apply protective copper fungicides or labeled captan sprays in early spring if leaf scorch was severe in the prior season
Do not spray copper during bloom to protect pollinators and prevent fruit marking
Follow all local extension recommendations, label dilution rates, and pre-harvest intervals

Strawberry___healthy.description: The strawberry foliage displays healthy, glossy, rich green trifoliolate leaves with clean serrated margins, robust petioles, and no signs of leaf spot, scorch, or spider mite bronzing.
symptoms: Glossy, dark green trifoliolate leaves with crisp, intact margins
No purple leaf spots, brown scorch patches, or powdery mildew coatings
Clean leaf petioles and healthy runner/crown development
possible_causes: Healthy disease-free runners, raised bed cultivation, clean straw mulch, and drip irrigation
prevention: Maintain fresh straw mulch under fruit and leaves to prevent soil-splash contamination
Renovate strawberry beds annually after the main harvest season
Scout regularly for spider mites, slugs, and early fungal leaf spots
care_recommendations: Provide regular, consistent drip watering during flowering and fruit ripening
Keep strawberry rows narrow (30–45 cm) to maintain good airflow and ease of picking
Remove dead or yellowing leaves periodically to keep the bed clean
safe_treatment: No treatment needed. Continue good strawberry bed management

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Tomato bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species. It produces small, water-soaked dark spots on leaves, stems, and green fruit, leading to heavy defoliation and unmarketable fruit.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black, water-soaked circular spots on leaves (usually 1–3 mm wide)
Leaf spots may be surrounded by yellow halos; centers can dry and tear, giving a ragged look
Infected leaves turn brown, wither, and drop prematurely, leading to sunscald on fruit
Small, raised, scab-like black blisters or crusty spots on green tomato fruits
possible_causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas species introduced through contaminated seed or infected transplants
Warm temperatures (24–30°C) with frequent rainstorms, heavy dew, or overhead irrigation
Bacteria spread rapidly by splashing water droplets, wind-driven rain, and farm tools
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot-water treated seeds
Plant resistant tomato hybrids when available for your region
Rotate crops for at least 2–3 years away from tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants
Disinfect stakes, trellises, and pruning tools regularly with a 10% bleach or alcohol solution
care_recommendations: Irrigate at the base using drip lines; strictly avoid overhead sprinkler watering
Stake and prune tomato vines to keep foliage upright and off the soil
Never cultivate, prune, or harvest tomatoes when the plants are wet with dew or rain
safe_treatment: Apply preventive copper bactericide combined with mancozeb early in the season when conditions favor disease
Bio-pesticides containing Bacillus subtilis or bacteriophages can provide protective suppression
Once bacterial spot is widespread, chemical control is limited; focus on strict sanitation and field hygiene
Follow all regional label guidelines and pre-harvest intervals

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Tomato early blight is a widespread fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It begins on older lower leaves, producing dark brown spots with characteristic concentric rings, and progresses upward.
symptoms: Circular to irregular dark brown spots starting on older lower foliage
Characteristic 'target-board' or bullseye pattern of concentric rings inside the spots
Yellowing (chlorosis) around the spots spreading across the leaflet, causing defoliation
Dark, sunken, leathery cankers on stems and near the stem-end of ripe fruit
possible_causes: Fungus Alternaria solani surviving in solanaceous crop residues, volunteer plants, or solanaceous weeds
Warm, humid weather (24–29°C) with alternating wet periods (rain or dew) and dry periods
Water splash from bare soil transferring fungal spores onto lower leaves
prevention: Practice a 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops (tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplants)
Mulch the soil around plants with straw, paper, or plastic to prevent soil splash onto lower foliage
Stake, cage, and prune plants to improve airflow and keep leaves off the ground
Prune off the bottom 25–30 cm of lower leaves once the plant is established
care_recommendations: Water only at the base using drip irrigation or soaker hoses early in the morning
Remove and safely dispose of infected lower leaves as soon as early spots appear
Clean up all tomato vine residues thoroughly after the final harvest
safe_treatment: Apply protective copper-based fungicides, bio-fungicides (Bacillus subtilis), or labeled protectants (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) starting when the first fruit clusters set or at the first sign of lower leaf spotting
Reapply according to label instructions during rainy periods
Observe label safety requirements and pre-harvest intervals

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a devastating disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It develops and spreads rapidly in cool, wet, humid weather, causing large greasy lesions, white mold, and plant death.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale to dark green lesions that rapidly turn brown or black
Delicate white, fuzzy mold growth visible on the undersides of leaves during humid mornings
Dark brown to black lesions girdling stems and leaf petioles
Large, firm, greasy-brown or olive-colored rotting patches on green and ripe tomato fruit
possible_causes: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans spread by wind-borne spores over long distances from infected potato or tomato fields
Cool (10–21°C), wet, overcast, or foggy weather with sustained high humidity (>90%)
Planting infected transplants or proximity to infected potato cull piles
prevention: Plant resistant tomato cultivars where available
Do not plant tomatoes in close proximity to potato plantings
Ensure wide plant spacing and sunny garden exposure to facilitate rapid canopy drying
Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants in the vicinity before the season begins
care_recommendations: Inspect plants twice weekly, especially after cool rainy weather
Use drip irrigation only; avoid wetting foliage
If late blight is confirmed on an isolated plant, bag and remove the entire plant immediately on a dry sunny day to prevent spore release
safe_treatment: Preventive applications of copper fungicides or registered protectants are crucial before symptoms appear when late blight warnings are active
Fungicides cannot cure heavily blighted plants; infected plants must be removed to protect the remaining crop
Consult local agricultural extension for immediate regional blight advisories and approved treatments

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is caused by Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum). It is especially prevalent in greenhouse, high tunnel, and sheltered environments where relative humidity frequently exceeds 85%.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow diffuse spots with indistinct borders on the upper surface of older leaves
Olive-green to velvety grayish-brown mold growth on the corresponding lower surface of the spots
Infected leaves gradually curl, wither, turn brown, and drop prematurely
Blossoms and green fruit may rarely show dark sunken rot, but main damage is defoliation
possible_causes: Fungus Passalora fulva thriving in warm (20–25°C), humid microclimates (relative humidity >85%)
Inadequate ventilation in high tunnels, greenhouses, or overcrowded garden beds
Prolonged leaf surface moisture from condensation or overhead watering
prevention: Maximize greenhouse or high tunnel ventilation with fans, roof vents, and side roll-ups
Space plants generously to promote constant air movement through the canopy
Select tomato cultivars with genetic resistance (Cf genes) to leaf mold races
Keep relative humidity below 85% through active heating and air circulation at night
care_recommendations: Prune off lower leaves and suckers up to the first fruit cluster to enhance bottom airflow
Water exclusively with drip irrigation; avoid splashing water on foliage
Disinfect greenhouse structures and stakes between cropping cycles
safe_treatment: Apply protective copper fungicides or bio-fungicides ensuring thorough coverage of leaf undersides
Ventilation and humidity management are generally far more effective than chemical control alone
Follow all product label safety guidelines and pre-harvest intervals

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It is one of the most common and destructive tomato foliage diseases, causing hundreds of tiny circular spots and rapid lower defoliation.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots (1.5–3 mm) appearing first on the lowest older leaves
Spots have dark brown borders and sunken grayish-white centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia fruiting bodies) are visible inside the gray centers with a hand lens
Leaves yellow around the spots, shrivel, and drop prematurely, moving progressively up the stem
possible_causes: Fungus Septoria lycopersici overwintering in fallen tomato debris, solanaceous weeds, and wooden stakes
Warm temperatures (20–27°C) accompanied by frequent rains, overhead watering, or heavy dew
Fungal spores splashed onto lower leaves from rain bouncing off unmulched soil
prevention: Rotate crops for at least 3 years away from tomatoes and related nightshade plants
Mulch bare soil with clean straw, paper, or plastic mulch to create a physical barrier against soil splash
Stake, cage, and prune tomato plants to maintain good distance between foliage and the ground
Prune lower foliage (bottom 30 cm) once plants are established
care_recommendations: Use drip irrigation or water at the base in early morning to keep leaves completely dry
Prune off and safely destroy spotted lower leaves as soon as symptoms first appear
Clean up and dispose of all tomato debris at the end of the season
safe_treatment: Apply protective copper fungicides, sulfur, or registered protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil) starting when lower leaves first show symptoms
Reapply according to label instructions during wet weather
Adhere strictly to product label directions and pre-harvest intervals

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are tiny sap-feeding arachnids. They thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions, piercing plant cells on the undersides of leaves and spinning fine protective webbing.
symptoms: Fine yellow, white, or silvery speckling (stippling) on the upper surface of leaves
Delicate silky webbing visible on leaf undersides, growing tips, and leaf axils
Leaves turn bronze or yellow, become dry and brittle, and drop prematurely
Tiny yellow, green, or reddish mites moving under webbing on the underside of leaves
possible_causes: Hot, dry, dusty weather conditions (temperatures above 30°C and low humidity)
Drought-stressed tomato plants that provide concentrated plant sugars to mites
Excessive broad-spectrum insecticide use that eliminates natural mite predators (ladybugs, lacewings, predatory mites)
prevention: Keep garden beds and nearby paths watered to minimize dust accumulation on foliage
Avoid broad-spectrum chemical insecticides (e.g. synthetic pyrethroids) that trigger mite outbreaks by killing predators
Inspect leaf undersides weekly using a 10x hand lens, especially along field edges
care_recommendations: Maintain consistent soil moisture to prevent drought stress
Wash dusty plants periodically with a targeted spray of water directed at leaf undersides in early morning
Conserve or introduce predatory mites (such as Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus)
safe_treatment: Spray insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or neem oil thoroughly coating the undersides of leaves early in the morning or evening
Repeat treatments every 5–7 days to target newly hatched mite generations
In commercial farming with severe pressure, use labeled selective miticides under extension guidance to avoid killing beneficial insects

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Tomato target spot is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It is common in warm, humid regions, producing brown circular lesions with concentric rings on leaves and sunken cratered lesions on fruit.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint brown spots on leaves that enlarge into circular lesions with concentric rings
Lesions often have a light brown center and dark margin, sometimes with a chlorotic yellow halo
Extensive leaf blighting and defoliation from the lower canopy upward
Fruit lesions start as small brown specks that become sunken, circular, and dark with cracked centers
possible_causes: Fungus Corynespora cassiicola surviving in crop debris, solanaceous weeds, and alternate hosts (papaya, cucumber, soybean)
Warm temperatures (20–30°C) combined with high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness
Overcrowded plant canopy restricting air movement
prevention: Increase plant spacing to maximize air movement and rapid leaf drying
Rotate crops away from tomatoes, peppers, and cucumbers for at least 2–3 years
Stake and prune plants to improve airflow through the lower canopy
Destroy all crop residues thoroughly after final harvest
care_recommendations: Irrigate using drip emitters rather than overhead sprinklers
Prune lower suckers and leaves touching the ground
Scout plants regularly during warm, rainy weather
safe_treatment: Apply protective copper fungicides or registered broad-spectrum fungicides according to regional extension recommendations
Begin protective sprays when weather conditions favor disease and maintain recommended intervals
Follow all product label safety guidelines and pre-harvest intervals

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a severe viral disease transmitted exclusively by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe leaf curling, stunting, and drastic flower drop.
symptoms: Leaves curl strongly upward and become cupped and distorted
Intense yellowing (chlorosis) along leaf margins and interveinal areas, especially on young leaves
Plants become severely stunted and take on a bushy, compact appearance
Flowers drop before fruit can set; infected young plants produce virtually no harvestable fruit
possible_causes: Geminivirus transmitted by adult whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) feeding on plant sap
Planting infected nursery transplants carrying the virus or harboring whitefly eggs
Warm, dry weather conditions that accelerate whitefly reproductive cycles
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato hybrids (labeled with TYLCV resistance)
Use fine 50-mesh insect netting over seedling nursery beds to exclude whiteflies
Use reflective silver or yellow plastic mulches that deter whiteflies from landing on young plants
Eradicate weeds in and around fields that serve as alternate hosts for whiteflies and the virus
care_recommendations: Immediately rogue out, bag, and destroy plants displaying early virus symptoms to prevent whiteflies from acquiring and spreading the virus
Monitor whitefly populations using yellow sticky cards placed throughout the crop
Coordinate whitefly management collectively across neighboring vegetable fields
safe_treatment: There is no chemical cure for plant viruses; infected plants cannot be cured
Control efforts must focus on managing the whitefly insect vector using insecticidal soaps, neem oil, or approved selective systemic insecticides in nurseries
Follow all local extension safety recommendations for whitefly management

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a highly stable and easily transmitted plant virus. It causes mottling, distorted leaves, and internal browning in fruit, spreading readily via mechanical contact and contaminated tools.
symptoms: Mottled pattern of alternating light green and dark green patches on leaves
Leaves may become distorted, crinkled, narrowed, or fern-like ('shoestring' symptom)
Overall plant stunting and delayed flowering
Fruit may display uneven ripening, yellowish blotches, and internal brown necrotic rings
possible_causes: Virus mechanically transmitted on hands, tools, stakes, and clothing during pruning and handling
Transmission through contaminated seed coats
Virus survives for years in dry plant debris and un-sanitized greenhouse equipment
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seeds and select tomato varieties with ToMV genetic resistance
Disinfect pruning shears, trellises, and stakes with a 10% household bleach solution or 20% non-fat dry milk solution
Workers should wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling plants; avoid tobacco use in tomato fields as tobacco can harbor mosaic viruses
Do not save seed from plants showing any mosaic symptoms
care_recommendations: Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately upon detection; do not compost infected plants
Handle healthy plants first before touching suspect plants during routine field operations
Clean up and safely dispose of all crop residues at the end of the season
safe_treatment: There is no chemical treatment to cure viral infections in plants
Control relies strictly on preventive sanitation, resistant cultivars, and removing infected plants
Focus entirely on strict hygiene and tool disinfection

Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato foliage exhibits healthy, deep green compound leaves with firm leaflets, clear veins, and natural glandular hairs, free of leaf spot, blight, curling, or mite damage.
symptoms: Deep, uniform green color across compound leaflets
No dark target spots, water-soaked lesions, yellow cupping, or mosaic mottling
Sturdy green stems and healthy, vigorous flower cluster development
possible_causes: Disease-resistant cultivars, good crop rotation, consistent drip watering, balanced fertilization, and good weed control
prevention: Maintain soil mulching to prevent soil-splash pathogens
Prune lower foliage and suckers to encourage good airflow and trellis support
Scout plants weekly for early signs of hornworms, whiteflies, or blight
care_recommendations: Maintain consistent drip irrigation to avoid blossom end rot and fruit splitting
Provide balanced tomato fertilizer with adequate calcium, potassium, and phosphorus
Ensure sturdy staking or caging to keep vines and fruit elevated above the ground
safe_treatment: No chemical intervention needed. Maintain sound cultural management
